claim: Most reagents available for loss-of-function (LOF) and gain-of-function studies using RNAi or CRISPR rely on GAL4/UAS-mediated expression.
source: Most reagents available for loss-of-function (LOF) and gain-of-function studies using RNAi or CRISPR rely on GAL4/UAS-mediated expression (Brand and Perrimon, 1993; Dietzl et al., 2007; Perkins et al., 2015; Zirin et al., 2020; Port and Boutros, 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature describing GAL4/UAS-based reagents.

claim: Some studies, such as the study of intercellular or inter-organ communication, require the simultaneous use of two independent binary transcriptional systems.
source: However, some studies, such as the study of intercellular or inter-organ communication, require the simultaneous use of two independent binary transcriptional systems.
evidence: Based on established scientific understanding of experimental requirements for multi-tissue studies.

claim: Dual expression systems have been used to study how a Drosophila insulin-like peptide released from the wing primordium communicates with the brain to control organ growth.
source: For example, dual expression systems have been used to study how a Drosophila insulin-like peptide released from the wing primordium communicates with the brain to control organ growth (Colombani et al., 2015), analyze signaling from olfactory neurons to blood cells (Shim et al., 2013), independently manipulate ligand-producing and ligand receiving cells (Yagi et al., 2010), and visualize interactions between clonal cell populations in tissues (Bosch et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Colombani et al., 2015.

claim: Dual expression systems have been used to analyze signaling from olfactory neurons to blood cells.
source: For example, dual expression systems have been used to study how a Drosophila insulin-like peptide released from the wing primordium communicates with the brain to control organ growth (Colombani et al., 2015), analyze signaling from olfactory neurons to blood cells (Shim et al., 2013), independently manipulate ligand-producing and ligand receiving cells (Yagi et al., 2010), and visualize interactions between clonal cell populations in tissues (Bosch et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shim et al., 2013.

claim: Dual expression systems have been used to independently manipulate ligand-producing and ligand receiving cells.
source: For example, dual expression systems have been used to study how a Drosophila insulin-like peptide released from the wing primordium communicates with the brain to control organ growth (Colombani et al., 2015), analyze signaling from olfactory neurons to blood cells (Shim et al., 2013), independently manipulate ligand-producing and ligand receiving cells (Yagi et al., 2010), and visualize interactions between clonal cell populations in tissues (Bosch et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yagi et al., 2010.

claim: Dual expression systems have been used to visualize interactions between clonal cell populations in tissues.
source: For example, dual expression systems have been used to study how a Drosophila insulin-like peptide released from the wing primordium communicates with the brain to control organ growth (Colombani et al., 2015), analyze signaling from olfactory neurons to blood cells (Shim et al., 2013), independently manipulate ligand-producing and ligand receiving cells (Yagi et al., 2010), and visualize interactions between clonal cell populations in tissues (Bosch et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bosch et al., 2015.

claim: The LexA/LexAop system has been developed for simultaneous manipulation of different sets of cells in a given tissue.
source: Based on the need to simultaneously manipulate different sets of cells in a given tissue, the LexA/LexAop system (Lai and Lee, 2006) and the QF/QUAS system (Potter et al., 2010; Potter and Luo, 2011) have been developed.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lai and Lee, 2006.

claim: The QF/QUAS system has been developed for simultaneous manipulation of different sets of cells in a given tissue.
source: Based on the need to simultaneously manipulate different sets of cells in a given tissue, the LexA/LexAop system (Lai and Lee, 2006) and the QF/QUAS system (Potter et al., 2010; Potter and Luo, 2011) have been developed.
evidence: Supported by citations to Potter et al., 2010 and Potter and Luo, 2011.

claim: There have been no systematic studies comparing the LexA and QF systems.
source: There have been no systematic studies comparing the two systems, with only anecdotal evidence to support one system over the other.
evidence: Statement about the absence of systematic comparative studies in the literature.

claim: The numbers of available LexA and QF fly lines with tissue-specific expression domains are far lower than that represented by the thousands of GAL4 enhancer lines.
source: The numbers of available LexA and QF fly lines with tissue-specific expression domains are far lower than that represented by the thousands of GAL4 enhancer lines, which have been developed using various approaches over the past 25 years.
evidence: Based on knowledge of available fly stock resources.

claim: The largest existing set of LexA system driver lines were produced by the Janelia FlyLight Project and Vienna Tiles Project.
source: The largest existing set of LexA system driver lines were produced by the Janelia FlyLight Project and Vienna Tiles Project (Jenett et al., 2012; Tirian and Dickson, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jenett et al., 2012 and Tirian and Dickson, 2017.

claim: FlyLight lines were developed primarily for nervous system expression.
source: However, these lines were developed primarily for nervous system expression.
evidence: Based on knowledge of the FlyLight Project's focus.

claim: FlyLight lines are not well suited for experiments targeting non-neuronal cell types.
source: Although they are often expressed in other tissues, they are not well suited for experiments targeting non-neuronal cell types.
evidence: Inferred from the primary nervous system focus of FlyLight lines.

claim: The FlyLight lines use a p65 transcriptional activation domain and therefore are not compatible with the GAL80 temperature-sensitive GAL4 repression system.
source: Furthermore, the FlyLight lines use a p65 transcriptional activation domain and therefore are not compatible with the GAL80 temperature-sensitive GAL4 repression system.
evidence: Based on knowledge of the incompatibility between p65 activation domain and GAL80 repression.

claim: A second large collection of ~180 LexA-based enhancer trap fly stocks has been generated (the StanEx collection).
source: A second large collection of ~180 LexA-based enhancer trap fly stocks has been generated (the StanEx collection) (Kockel et al., 2016; Kockel et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kockel et al., 2016, 2019 and Kim et al., 2023.

claim: On average, each StanEx line expresses LexA activity in five distinct cell types.
source: On average, each StanEx line expresses LexA activity in five distinct cell types, with only one line showing expression in just one tissue, unfortunately limiting usefulness of these reagents (Kockel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kockel et al., 2016.

claim: Only one StanEx line shows expression in just one tissue.
source: On average, each StanEx line expresses LexA activity in five distinct cell types, with only one line showing expression in just one tissue, unfortunately limiting usefulness of these reagents (Kockel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kockel et al., 2016.

claim: Enhancers very rarely produce expression patterns that are limited to a single cell type in a complex organism.
source: These findings are consistent with prior studies indicating that enhancers very rarely produce expression patterns that are limited to a single cell type in a complex organism (Jenett et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jenett et al., 2012.

claim: There are 101 total QF lines available from the Bloomington Drosophila Stock Center (BDSC).
source: Regarding the Q system, there are 101 total QF lines available from the Bloomington Drosophila Stock Center (BDSC).
evidence: Based on knowledge of available stock center resources.

claim: The original QF can be toxic when expressed at high levels.
source: As the original QF can be toxic when expressed at high levels (Potter et al., 2010), second-generation QF2 and QF2w, which are much less toxic and can be expressed broadly in vivo, were generated (Riabinina et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Potter et al., 2010.

claim: Second-generation QF2 and QF2w are much less toxic than the original QF and can be expressed broadly in vivo.
source: As the original QF can be toxic when expressed at high levels (Potter et al., 2010), second-generation QF2 and QF2w, which are much less toxic and can be expressed broadly in vivo, were generated (Riabinina et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Riabinina et al., 2015.

claim: Among the 51 QF2 and QF2w lines available at BDSC, most are expressed in the brain.
source: Among the 51 QF2 and QF2w lines available at BDSC, most are expressed in the brain, with relatively few of these drivers expressed specifically in other tissues.
evidence: Based on knowledge of available BDSC stock characteristics.

claim: There remains an unmet need for more LexA and QF drivers with tissue-specific expression patterns.
source: Thus, there remains an unmet need for more LexA and QF drivers with tissue-specific expression patterns.
evidence: Inferred from the limited availability and specificity of existing drivers.

claim: There are only ~260 LexA driver-compatible LexAop stocks available at BDSC.
source: Furthermore, there are only ~260 LexA driver-compatible LexAop and ~130 QF driver-compatible QUAS stocks available at BDSC.
evidence: Based on knowledge of available BDSC stock resources.

claim: There are only ~130 QF driver-compatible QUAS stocks available at BDSC.
source: Furthermore, there are only ~260 LexA driver-compatible LexAop and ~130 QF driver-compatible QUAS stocks available at BDSC.
evidence: Based on knowledge of available BDSC stock resources.

claim: The vast majority of LexAop and QUAS stocks are to induce expression of fluorescent reporter genes, rather than molecular genetic reagents such as shRNAs for RNAi.
source: The vast majority of these are to induce expression of fluorescent reporter genes, rather than molecular genetic reagents such as shRNAs for RNAi.
evidence: Based on knowledge of the composition of available stock collections.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 technology makes it possible to knock-in a transcriptional activator into any locus.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 technology now makes it possible to knock-in a transcriptional activator into any locus.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of CRISPR/Cas9 capabilities.

claim: Some groups have described tools to swap QF or LexA into the GAL4 coding region of existing GAL4 enhancer trap lines.
source: Some groups have also recently described tools to swap QF or LexA into the GAL4 coding region of existing GAL4 enhancer trap lines (Lin and Potter, 2016; Chang et al., 2022; Karuparti et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lin and Potter, 2016; Chang et al., 2022; Karuparti et al., 2023.

claim: The frequency of conversion can vary greatly among different GAL4 lines when swapping QF or LexA into GAL4 coding regions.
source: The conversion can be performed through genetic crosses; however, the frequency of conversion can vary greatly among different GAL4 lines, and many such swaps do not fully reproduce the original GAL4 expression patterns (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019.

claim: Many swaps of QF or LexA into GAL4 coding regions do not fully reproduce the original GAL4 expression patterns.
source: The conversion can be performed through genetic crosses; however, the frequency of conversion can vary greatly among different GAL4 lines, and many such swaps do not fully reproduce the original GAL4 expression patterns (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019.

claim: The authors targeted 23 genes to produce 44 new highly tissue-specific LexA-GAD and QF2 driver lines by CRISPR-mediated homology-directed repair.
source: Focusing on genes with well-characterized GAL4 expression patterns, we targeted 23 genes to produce 44 new highly tissue-specific LexA-GAD and QF2 driver lines by CRISPR-mediated homology-directed repair.
evidence: Direct statement of the experimental work performed in this study.

claim: The authors chose to use LexA with the GAL4 activation domain to allow for temporal control by the temperature-sensitive GAL4 repressor, GAL80.
source: We chose to use LexA with the GAL4 activation domain, rather than the p65 or VP16 activation domains to allow for temporal control by the temperature-sensitive GAL4 repressor, GAL80 (Lai and Lee, 2006; Pfeiffer et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lai and Lee, 2006 and Pfeiffer et al., 2010, explaining the rationale for the choice.

claim: The authors chose to use QF2 variant over the original QF to avoid the toxicity reported for the latter.
source: We chose to use QF2 variant over the original QF, to avoid the toxicity reported for the latter (Riabinina et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Riabinina et al., 2015.

claim: QF2 activity can be regulated temporally by expressing QS, a QF repressor.
source: Like GAL80-based modulation of LexA-GAD, QF2 activity can also be regulated temporally by expressing QS, a QF repressor.
evidence: Based on knowledge of QF2 regulation mechanisms.

claim: QS repression of QF can be released by feeding flies quinic acid.
source: QS repression of QF can be released by feeding flies quinic acid (Riabinina and Potter, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Riabinina and Potter, 2016.

claim: Each knock-in was rigorously genotyped, and the expression pattern verified by imaging.
source: Each knock-in was rigorously genotyped, and the expression pattern verified by imaging.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental validation performed.

claim: The authors can systematically compare LexA-GAD vs QF2 activators inserted at precisely the same position in the genome.
source: Thus, we can systematically compare LexA-GAD vs QF2 activators inserted at precisely the same position in the genome.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental design of inserting both activators at the same genomic positions.

claim: The authors constructed vectors that encode QF2 and LexA-GAD transcription factors in a single vector, with each coding sequence flanked by FRT sites.
source: This includes constructs that encode QF2 and LexA-GAD transcription factors in a single vector, with each coding sequence flanked by FRT sites.
evidence: Direct statement of construct design.

claim: Following successful integration into the fly genome, the double driver vector generates a driver in which a target gene expresses both QF2 and LexA-GAD.
source: Following successful integration into the fly genome, the vector generates a driver in which a target gene expresses both QF2 and LexA-GAD.
evidence: Direct statement of the functional outcome of the construct.

claim: One of the two coding regions in the double driver can be excised with Flp, resulting in flies that express only QF2 or LexA-GAD.
source: If desired, one of the two coding regions can then be excised with Flp, resulting in flies that express only QF2 or LexA-GAD.
evidence: Direct statement of the experimental strategy for generating single drivers from double drivers.

claim: The authors evaluated both QF2 and LexA-GAD systems for in vivo gene knockdown.
source: Furthermore, we evaluated both QF2 and LexA-GAD systems for in vivo gene knockdown and are generating a compatible library of transgenic shRNA lines in our custom QUAS and LexAop vectors as a community resource.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental work performed.

claim: The authors are generating a library of transgenic shRNA lines in custom QUAS and LexAop vectors as a community resource.
source: Furthermore, we evaluated both QF2 and LexA-GAD systems for in vivo gene knockdown and are generating a compatible library of transgenic shRNA lines in our custom QUAS and LexAop vectors as a community resource.
evidence: Direct statement of ongoing resource generation.

claim: The authors made each genetic driver line by inserting T2A-LexA-GAD or T2A-QF2 in the coding sequence of a target gene.
source: We made each genetic driver line by inserting T2A-LexA-GAD or T2A-QF2 in the coding sequence of a target gene.
evidence: Direct statement of the experimental method used.

claim: The authors previously reported the CRISPaint method to insert T2A-GAL4 into any gene using homology-independent repair.
source: We have previously reported the CRISPaint method to insert T2A-GAL4 into any gene using homology-independent repair (Bosch et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bosch et al., 2020.

claim: The CRISPaint method showed robust gene-specific integration of donor plasmids in the fly germ line.
source: Using this method, we showed robust gene-specific integration of donor plasmids in the fly germ line and successfully generated new driver lines.
evidence: Direct statement of results from previous work.

claim: The CRISPaint method has a high probability of indels at the insertion site.
source: However, because of the high probability of indels at the insertion site, we opted to use traditional CRISPR homology-directed repair to insert the T2A-LexA-GAD and T2A-QF2 into the genome.
evidence: Direct statement of a limitation of the CRISPaint method.

claim: The authors opted to use the Hsp70 3'UTR because it is comparatively weaker than SV40 3'UTR and may avoid toxicity due to overexpression of LexA-GAD or QF2.
source: We opted to use the Hsp70 3'UTR, as opposed to SV40 3'UTR, because it is comparatively weaker and may avoid toxicity due to overexpression of LexA-GAD or QF2.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about avoiding toxicity based on the weaker nature of Hsp70 3'UTR.

claim: All the donor vectors contain a 3XP3-RFP transformation marker gene flanked by loxP sites.
source: All the vectors contain a 3XP3-RFP transformation marker gene flanked by loxP sites.
evidence: Direct statement of vector design feature.

claim: The donor vectors are compatible with two different cloning methods for making a CRISPR donor plasmid.
source: These vectors are compatible with two different cloning methods for making a CRISPR donor plasmid.
evidence: Direct statement of vector compatibility.

claim: In the long homology arm (HA) method, ~1000 bp HAs are amplified from genomic DNA and inserted into the donor plasmid by Gibson assembly.
source: In the long homology arm (HA) method (Figure 1B), ~1000 bp HAs are amplified from genomic DNA and inserted into the donor plasmid by Gibson assembly.
evidence: Direct statement of the cloning method, also shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the drop-in cloning method, a company synthesizes and clones a plasmid that contains all of the necessary features for CRISPR HDR plus a cloning site.
source: In the 'drop-in' cloning method (Figure 1C; Kanca et al., 2022), a company synthesizes and clones a plasmid that contains all of the necessary features for CRISPR HDR plus a cloning site to allow ligation of T2A-LexA-GAD, T2A-QF, or T2A-LexA-GAD-T2A-QF fragments in a single step to produce the donor plasmid.
evidence: Direct statement of the cloning method, supported by citation to Kanca et al., 2022 and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The authors selected a set of genes with tissue-specific expression patterns encompassing most of the major organs of the fly.
source: For our targets, we selected a set of genes with tissue-specific expression patterns encompassing most of the major organs of the fly (Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement of target gene selection criteria, with data shown in Table 1.

claim: The authors selected genes which had a previously characterized GAL4 insertion and strong evidence of tissue specificity.
source: When possible, we selected genes which had a previously characterized GAL4 insertion, and strong evidence of tissue specificity (e.g. from publicly available scRNAseq, in situ, and immunohistochemistry).
evidence: Direct statement of selection criteria.

claim: The authors selected integration sites in the most 5' coding exon common to all or most isoforms.
source: We selected integration sites in the most 5' coding exon common to all or most isoforms, resulting in expression of the activators under control of the endogenous gene regulatory regions.
evidence: Direct statement of the integration site selection strategy.

claim: The knock-in produces a truncated endogenous protein and thus a predicted strong LOF allele.
source: The knock-in also produces a truncated endogenous protein and thus a predicted strong LOF allele.
evidence: Inferred from the insertion strategy that disrupts the endogenous gene.

claim: The authors verified the knock-ins by PCR-amplifying the genomic regions flanking the insertion sites and confirming that the insertions were seamless and in-frame.
source: To verify the knock-ins, we PCR-amplified the genomic regions flanking the insertion sites and confirmed that the insertions were seamless and in-frame.
evidence: Direct statement of the verification method used.

claim: Most of the knock-in stocks were made with the long HA method.
source: Most of our knock-in stocks were made with the long HA method, but we transitioned to the drop-in method as this technology became available.
evidence: Direct statement of the methods used.

claim: The authors were able to successfully generate knock-ins into nearly all the target genes using the long HA and drop-in methods.
source: As Table 1 shows, we were able to successfully generate knock-ins into nearly all the target genes using these methods.
evidence: Direct statement of results, with data shown in Table 1.

claim: Most of the T2A-LexA-GAD and T2A-QF2 knock-in lines are highly tissue-specific.
source: Note that most of the lines are highly tissue-specific and are comparable between the LexA-GAD and QF2 knock-ins.
evidence: Direct statement of observed results from imaging experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The expression patterns are comparable between the LexA-GAD and QF2 knock-ins for most lines.
source: Note that most of the lines are highly tissue-specific and are comparable between the LexA-GAD and QF2 knock-ins.
evidence: Direct statement of observed results from imaging experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Insertions in the daughterless gene (da) are an exception, as the T2A-LexA-GAD, but not the T2A-QF2, gives the expected ubiquitous expression pattern.
source: Insertions in the daughterless gene (da) are an exception, as the T2A-LexA-GAD (Figure 2A), but not the T2A-QF2 (Figure 2B), gives the expected ubiquitous expression pattern.
evidence: Direct statement of observed results from imaging experiments shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: For insertions in the nubbin gene (nub), the T2A-LexA-GAD, but not the T2A-QF2, gives the expected expression in the wing imaginal disc.
source: Similarly, for insertions in the nubbin gene (nub) the T2A-LexA-GAD (Figure 2LL), but not the T2A-QF2 (Figure 2MM), gives the expected expression in the wing imaginal disc.
evidence: Direct statement of observed results from imaging experiments shown in Figure 2LL and 2MM.

claim: In both da and nub cases, T2A-QF is expressed in the correct tissues, but incompletely.
source: In both cases, T2A-QF is expressed in the correct tissues, but incompletely.
evidence: Direct statement of observed results from imaging experiments.

claim: The patterns are remarkably consistent between the T2A-LexA-GAD and T2A-QF2 knock-in lines overall.
source: Even with these exceptions, the patterns are remarkably consistent between the T2A-LexA-GAD and T2A-QF2 knock-in lines overall.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the overall consistency of expression patterns.

claim: The 3XP3-RFP marker expresses red fluorescence in the larval gut and anal pad, and the adult eye.
source: Our donor plasmids contain the transgenesis marker 3XP3-RFP, which expresses red fluorescence in the larval gut and anal pad, and the adult eye (Berghammer et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Berghammer et al., 1999.

claim: The authors sometimes observed LexA-Gad or QF2 expression in the larval anal pad and gut, coincident with expression of RFP.
source: Like our previous knock-ins using the CRISPaint method (Bosch et al., 2020), we sometimes observed LexA-Gad or QF2 expression in the larval anal pad and gut, coincident with expression of RFP.
evidence: Direct statement of observed results, with reference to previous work (Bosch et al., 2020).

claim: In the repo gene, T2A-QF2 is expressed in the expected glial cells, but also misexpressed in RFP positive cells.
source: Figure 3 shows one such example in the repo gene, where T2A-QF2 is expressed in the expected glial cells, but also misexpressed in RFP positive cells.
evidence: Direct statement of observed results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The influence of the 3XP3-RFP is not observed in T2A-LexA-GAD repo knock-in animals.
source: Interestingly, this influence of the 3XP3-RFP is not observed in T2A-LexA-GAD repo knock-in animals (Figure 2I).
evidence: Direct statement of observed results shown in Figure 2I.

claim: In the breathless (btl) gene, misexpression of LexA-GAD, but not QF2, is observed in RFP positive cells.
source: Conversely, in the breathless (btl) gene, we observe misexpression of LexA-GAD, but not QF2 in RFP positive cells (Figure 2M and N).
evidence: Direct statement of observed results shown in Figure 2M and N.

claim: When the 3XP3-RFP cassette was removed in the repo knock-in by cre-lox recombination, misexpression of QF2 in the gut and anal pad was completely eliminated, while the glial expression remained.
source: Importantly, when we removed the 3XP3-RFP cassette in the repo knock-in by cre-lox recombination, misexpression of QF2 in the gut and anal pad was completely eliminated, while the glial expression remained (Figure 3B).
evidence: Direct statement of observed results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The authors have removed or are in the process of removing the 3XP3-RFP marker from all the knock-in stocks.
source: We therefore have removed or are in the process of removing the 3XP3-RFP marker from all the knock-in stocks.
evidence: Direct statement of ongoing work.

claim: The authors have successfully removed the 3XP3-RFP marker from 32 of the 41 driver lines that used this marker.
source: Currently, we have successfully removed it from 32 of the 41 driver lines that used this marker (Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement of results, with data shown in Table 1.

claim: By combining both drivers into a single construct, the authors could halve the number of injections.
source: We reasoned that by combining both drivers into a single construct, we could halve the number of injections, one of the most labor-intensive and expensive parts of the process.
evidence: Logical inference about the efficiency gain from combining drivers.

claim: The authors built two types of vectors for combined expression of LexA-GAD and QF2 transcription factors.
source: For this combined expression of LexA-GAD and QF2 transcription factors, we built two types of vectors: (1) a CRISPR donor version, pHDR-T2A-QF2-T2A-LexA-GAD-3xP3-RFP, which is used to insert the cassette into an endogenous locus of interest (Figure 4A), and (2) a phiC31-attB version, pMCS-T2A-QF2-T2A-LexA-GAD-WALIUM20, which is used to clone an enhancer fragment of interest and is then integrated into an attP site in the fly's genome (Figure 4B).
evidence: Direct statement of vector construction, with schematics shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: The phiC31-attB-compatible constructs use mini-white, not 3XP3-RFP, as a marker gene.
source: Note that the phiC31-attB-compatible constructs use mini-white, not 3XP3-RFP, as a marker gene.
evidence: Direct statement of construct design feature.

claim: The authors generated CRISPR knock-ins into the elav and hedgehog (hh) genes using the double driver vectors.
source: Using these vectors, we generated CRISPR knock-ins into the elav and hedgehog (hh) genes and enhancer lines for the decapentaplegic (dpp) and insulin-like peptide 2 (Ilp2) (Figure 4F) genes.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental work performed.

claim: The authors generated enhancer lines for the decapentaplegic (dpp) and insulin-like peptide 2 (Ilp2) genes using the double driver vectors.
source: Using these vectors, we generated CRISPR knock-ins into the elav and hedgehog (hh) genes and enhancer lines for the decapentaplegic (dpp) and insulin-like peptide 2 (Ilp2) (Figure 4F) genes.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental work performed.

claim: The elav knock-in expressed both T2A-QF2 and T2A-LexA-GAD in the expected pattern in the larval nervous system.
source: The elav knock-in (Figure 4C) expressed both T2A-QF2 and T2A-LexA-GAD in the expected pattern in the larval nervous system.
evidence: Direct statement of observed results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The elav knock-in showed some weak non-specific expression of T2A-LexA-GAD in the somatic muscles.
source: However, we did see some weak non-specific expression of T2A-LexA-GAD in the somatic muscles.
evidence: Direct statement of observed results.

claim: The hh knock-in expressed both T2A-QF2 and T2A-LexA-GAD in the expected pattern in the posterior of the imaginal discs.
source: The hh knock-in (Figure 4D) expressed both T2A-QF2 and T2A-LexA-GAD in the expected pattern in the posterior of the imaginal discs.
evidence: Direct statement of observed results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In the hh knock-in, T2A-QF2, but not T2A-LexA-GAD, was restricted from the wing pouch.
source: However, we observed that T2A-QF2, but not T2A-LexA-GAD, was restricted from the wing pouch, similar to the individual nub knock-ins (Figure 4D and Figure 2LL–MM).
evidence: Direct statement of observed results shown in Figure 4D and Figure 2LL-MM.

claim: The dpp enhancer directed expression of both T2A-QF2 and T2A-LexA-GAD along the anterior/posterior margin of the wing imaginal disc.
source: As expected, the dpp enhancer (Figure 4E) directed expression of both T2A-QF2 and T2A-LexA-GAD along the anterior/posterior margin of the wing imaginal disc.
evidence: Direct statement of observed results shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In the dpp enhancer line, T2A-QF was much reduced in the wing pouch.
source: Again, however, T2A-QF was much reduced in the wing pouch.
evidence: Direct statement of observed results.

claim: The Ilp2 enhancer directed expression of both T2A-QF2 and T2A-LexA-GAD very specifically in the insulin-producing cells of the larval brain.
source: Finally, the Ilp2 enhancer (Figure 4F) directed expression of both T2A-QF2 and T2A-LexA-GAD very specifically in the insulin-producing cells of the larval brain.
evidence: Direct statement of observed results shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The double driver constructs can effectively drive expression of both activators simultaneously in the target tissue, with the caveat that T2A-QF2 does not express well in the wing pouch.
source: Taken together, these results show that the double driver constructs can effectively drive expression of both activators simultaneously in the target tissue, with the caveat that T2A-QF2 does not express well in the wing pouch.
evidence: Summary statement of observed results from multiple experiments.

claim: FRT3 and FRT are mutually incompatible target sites for the Flp recombinase.
source: FRT3 and FRT are mutually incompatible target sites for the Flp recombinase: FRT3 can recombine with another FRT3, and FRT with FRT, but FRT3 cannot recombine with FRT.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of FRT site specificity.

claim: When recombined in cis, mutually incompatible FRT target sites randomly excise one of two inserts.
source: When recombined in cis, these mutually incompatible FRT target sites randomly excise one of two inserts (see Bosch et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bosch et al., 2015.

claim: Flp expression will result in the formation of either T2A-FRT3-LexA-GAD-FRT or T2A-FRT3-QF2-FRT.
source: Hence, Flp expression will result in the formation of either T2A-FRT3-LexA-GAD-FRT (caused by recombination between FRT3 sites) or T2A-FRT3-QF2-FRT (if recombination occurs between FRT sites).
evidence: Inferred from the mechanism of FRT/Flp recombination.

claim: Both recombination products will be stable even in the presence of Flp because they lack a pair of compatible FRT sites.
